label: Title
notes: Open by separating the geometric object from the algorithmic choices. The convex hull is a smallest enclosing convex region, but for computation we usually need the boundary vertices in a consistent order. Tell students that every algorithm in this lecture is a different way to discover the same ordered certificate.

label: Motivation
notes: Motivate the hull as a reusable geometric compression. A robot arm envelope, a thin containing strip, a minimum box, and a visible shape outline are different questions, but they all ask which input points support the outside. This gives a practical reason to care about extreme points before any algorithm appears.

label: Convexity
notes: Give both equivalent mental models. The segment test is the direct definition students can inspect visually, while the half-plane intersection model explains why boundary edges have supporting lines. Convex hull algorithms keep asking which line, edge, or direction exposes the next piece of that boundary.

label: Boundary Extremes
notes: Pause on output format, because it prevents later confusion. The filled hull is a continuum of points, but the algorithm returns a cyclic vertex list. The hard part is not merely naming which points are extreme; students also need to understand why the order of those points is part of the certificate.

label: Orientation
notes: Make the determinant feel like the chapter's vocabulary. It is twice a signed triangle area, so its sign tells us whether the third point lies left, right, or on the directed line. From here onward, every algorithmic decision can be translated into a repeated orientation question.

label: Triangle Witness
notes: Use the notebook visual as a certificate, not as decoration. A nonextreme point is proved nonextreme by a specific triangle of other points that contains it. This deliberately slow idea helps students see what is being discarded before the lecture moves to edge-based and output-sensitive methods.

label: Gift Wrapping Setup
notes: Connect the static edge test to Jarvis style wrapping. If a directed candidate edge leaves every point on the permitted side, it belongs to the hull. Gift wrapping does this test repeatedly: from the current vertex, rotate the candidate until no point lies outside the exposed side.

label: Gift Cost
notes: Name the variable h explicitly as the number of output vertices. Gift wrapping pays for one full scan per edge it reports, which is ideal when the boundary is tiny and painful when most points are on the boundary. This slide sets up the search for algorithms with different cost profiles.

label: QuickHull
notes: Present QuickHull as a filtering algorithm. It uses a farthest point to create two new candidate edges and a triangle that can be thrown away. The important invariant is that only points outside the exposed triangle can still affect the boundary, while the caution is that the recursion can be badly balanced.

label: Comparison
notes: Use the side-by-side artifact to reset the narrative. The three methods look different, yet the check confirms that they identify the same hull on the notebook data. Ask students to focus on each method's invariant: wrapping uses exposed edges, QuickHull uses discard regions, and Graham uses a stack of legal turns.

label: Graham Setup
notes: Separate Graham scan into a setup phase and a stack phase. The sort by polar angle is the expensive global operation, and it creates a traversal order where local orientation tests are enough. Tie handling belongs in the setup, because collinear rays can otherwise put the wrong point on the stack.

label: Graham Stack
notes: Emphasize the invariant rather than the mechanics alone. At any moment the stack is supposed to be the hull of points already encountered in angular order. A right turn exposes a concavity, so the middle stack point cannot remain on the processed-prefix hull and is popped before the new point is accepted.

label: Robustness
notes: This is the engineering checkpoint. The abstract algorithms assume clean inputs, but real inputs contain duplicate points, collinear runs, and nearly zero determinants. The goal is not to pretend these cases vanish; it is to choose conventions and arithmetic that make the output certificate match the intended hull.

label: Lower Bound
notes: Make the reduction concrete. Put each input number on the parabola y equals x squared. Because the curve is strictly convex, the hull chain exposes the points in increasing x order. Therefore an ordered hull routine would sort the numbers, so ordered hull output cannot beat the sorting lower bound in the comparison model.

label: Beyond Graham
notes: Use this slide as a map beyond the three central algorithms. Incremental insertion and divide-and-conquer both depend on tangent certificates, just in different workflows. Once students trust tangent walks on ordered hulls, rotating calipers, onion layers, and output-sensitive improvements become natural continuations rather than unrelated tricks.

label: Recap Lab
notes: Close by tying the checks back to the lecture goals. Students should be able to define the hull, identify extreme points, explain the orientation predicate, and compare the algorithmic invariants. The lab question asks them to vary the hull size h, because that is the parameter that makes output sensitivity visible.
